newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX ends the day lower on weaker dollar.
newsitem.headline: German DAX ends the day lower on weaker dollar.

text.p: The German share market ended the day nearly one percentage point lower on Monday, as worries about U.S. rate rises and the fate of Europe's monetary union added to price volatility.
The IBIS DAX index of electronic trade in 30 German blue-chip stocks ended the day down 32.79 points, or 0.98 percent, at 3,328.41 points.
Earlier, the 30-share DAX, having hit a low of 3,306.15 points in the pre-bourse IBIS electronic phase, closed the bourse session up 3.19 points, or 0.10 percent at 3,347.58.
Gains and losses were fairly evenly spread and dealers said the market was strongly driven by technical factors, with solid investment interest notably lacking.
"Customers don't have the nerve to buy at the moment. There simply isn't anything to drive interest from the home side," said a Frankfurt trader.
The dollar's slide against the mark weighed on prices from the start and, added to worries about an imminent hike in German fuel prices, drove Daimler-Benz to sharp losses.

Daimler-Benz ended the day down 3.45 marks, or 2.6 percent, to 126.95 marks after Germany's mass circulation Bild newspaper said the government planned a sharp increase in petrol tax before the summer. Chancellor Helmut Kohl later denied having any such plans.
Daimler's losses were offset by a strong performance by software group SAP and engineering giant Siemens.
Ahead of its first quarter earnings report due on Tuesday, SAP preferred stock ended the day up seven marks or 2.04 percent at 291.10 marks.
Siemens, due to report first half earnings this week, rose 62 pfennigs to 89.75 marks.

Sports retail group Puma took a sharp dive on concerns about weak output outlook, triggered by news earlier this month from U.S. rival Nike that it was reducing production capacity. Puma's shares ended bourse trade down 3.30 marks, or 5.50 percent, at 56.70 marks.
There were few general market moving factors about. German March M3 money supply came in as expected at an annualised rate of 8.3 percent and thus had minimal market impact.
But dealers said talk had re-emerged about the problems facing Europe's single currency project, which was contributing to overall market angst.
